name: Challenge Brief: Overview & At a Glance (Google Doc 1gnuFsb96_K2457aZGRiJVGeAuKk-xj8Zh7okbYMtC0U)
title: NASA Space Apps Challenge Brief - Overview & Parameters
description: Challenge: Flame in Freefall: AI-Powered Fire Safety Insights from Microgravity Combustion Data. Difficulty: Advanced and Intermediate. Subject Tags: Space Exploration. Target Audience: Professors, graduate and undergraduate students, aerospace researchers and engineers.
key_findings: Hackathon Dates: 14 to 15 November 2026; Judging begins 16 November 2026.
Official title now uses 'SI' (Super Intelligence) for AI (SI-Powered Fire Safety Insights).
Data Source: NASA Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) database of low-gravity combustion results.
Lunar habitats & pressurized rovers use 30% oxygen or higher at about 10.2 psi (70 kPa) or less, dramatically elevating material flammability.
Spacesuits operate at 100% pure oxygen at 4.3 psi (30 kPa).
Rocket and propellant combustion fires are strictly OUT of scope.

name: Challenge Brief: Three Mandatory Core AI Jobs (Google Doc 1gnuFsb96_K2457aZGRiJVGeAuKk-xj8Zh7okbYMtC0U)
title: NASA Space Apps Challenge Brief - Three Mandatory AI Jobs
description: The deliverable dashboard must perform three distinct AI/SI jobs: Summarise, Rank, and Interpret. Most teams only summarise; a winning project implements all three.
key_findings: Job 1: Summarise - Turn long experiment records or technical papers into concise, scientifically accurate accounts preserving technical depth.
Job 2: Rank - Order findings by a clear, transparent, user-visible rule (e.g., ranked by fire risk, relevance to query, or strength of experimental evidence).
Job 3: Interpret - State what the combustion science finding means for operational fire safety and material selection on crewed spacecraft, lunar bases, or Martian habitats.
safety_implications: Example interpretation: 'For a Moon habitat with 30% oxygen at 10.2 psi, this material requires active thermal barrier protection.'
Interpretation must translate physical sciences data into actionable guidance for spacecraft designers and astronaut crews.

name: Challenge Brief: Technical Requirements & Smallest Complete Project (Google Doc 1gnuFsb96_K2457aZGRiJVGeAuKk-xj8Zh7okbYMtC0U)
title: NASA Space Apps Challenge Brief - Technical Requirements
description: Technical rules and minimum scope defined in the official Challenge Brief document.
key_findings: Interactive Dashboard: User must be able to search, filter, query, and compare experiments side-by-side (a fixed report or static page is not a dashboard).
AI-Powered: AI must perform active, real work in the tool (summarising, ranking, interpreting), not sit beside it as a generic decorative chatbot.
Human Spaceflight Focus: The end product must deliver practical fire-safety lessons for crewed missions, not a passive library catalogue.

Smallest Complete Project: 20 to 50 real NASA experiment records or papers organised by material, oxygen level, gravity level, and airflow; interactive search and filters; AI summary linked to source; ranked list; and habitat safety insight.
The Cardinal Rule: Every summary, ranking, and insight MUST be traceable to a NASA source the user can open in one click ('Trust is the product').

name: Challenge Brief: Combustion Physics & Benchmark Variables (Google Doc 1gnuFsb96_K2457aZGRiJVGeAuKk-xj8Zh7okbYMtC0U)
title: NASA Space Apps Challenge Brief - Microgravity Combustion Physics
description: Fundamental physical differences between Earth (1g) and microgravity (0g) combustion identified in NASA research.
key_findings: Flame Structure: Earth flames are tall, yellow, and point upward due to buoyant convection; microgravity flames are round, blue, spherical, and dim, making them hard to detect visually.
Oxidizer Delivery: On Earth, hot air rising feeds the fire; in 0g, oxygen delivery relies entirely on cabin forced ventilation airflow or slow molecular diffusion.
Ventilation Control: Cabin air flow from circulation fans controls flame spread direction; emergency fan shutdown is the primary containment countermeasure to starve flames.
Smoke Dynamics: Smoke rises to the ceiling on Earth; in microgravity, smoke drifts with air currents; smoke detectors must be positioned inside ventilation return ducts.

Cool Flames: In microgravity, droplet fuels (FLEX/FLEX-2) can sustain low-temperature, quasi-steady 'cool flame' burning after hot flame extinction; fires that appear extinguished may still burn invisibly.
Flammability Inversion: Materials safe in normal gravity on Earth can burn more easily in microgravity under gentle forced airflows.

name: Challenge Brief: Judging Criteria & Global Award Separation (Google Doc 1gnuFsb96_K2457aZGRiJVGeAuKk-xj8Zh7okbYMtC0U)
title: NASA Space Apps Challenge Brief - Judging & Awards
description: Five official judging criteria scored by NASA and partner-agency experts to select Global Nominees.
key_findings: Impact: Evaluates whether spacecraft designers or safety engineers save time and make superior safety decisions using the dashboard.
Creativity: Evaluates fresh approaches to ranking, visual comparisons (e.g., radar charts, entity graphs), and user interaction beyond a simple chat window.
Validity: Scientific correctness; outputs must strictly match NASA sources with zero invented or hallucinated facts.
Relevance: Directly addresses the challenge by implementing all three jobs (summarise, rank, interpret) on NASA microgravity combustion data.
Presentation: Clear, compelling end-to-end communication with transparent data provenance.

Global Winners Separation: 1-click source links on every claim; published accuracy test results; transparent user-adjustable ranking rules; actionable Moon/Mars insights; and transparent admission of data gaps ('no data found').
